en: Magma rises beneath Taal Volcano because subducting tectonic plates melt, building pressure until the rock explodes outward as lava and ash.
The northeast monsoon brings cool, dry air to the Philippines because high pressure over Siberia pushes winds toward the warmer, lower-pressure equatorial region.
Geothermal plants in Tiwi generate electricity by pumping cold water deep underground, where hot rocks heat it into steam that spins surface turbines.
The Cagayan River forms a delta at its mouth because slowing water loses the energy needed to carry soil, dropping sediment to build new land.
Tubbataha Reefs grow because tiny coral polyps extract calcium from seawater to build hard limestone skeletons, which accumulate over thousands of years.
The Valley Fault System triggers earthquakes when tectonic plates get stuck, causing stress to build up until the rocks suddenly snap and slip.
Typhoons like Pagasa form over warm Philippine seas because evaporating ocean water releases latent heat, powering strong winds that spiral around a calm eye.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River expanded because slightly acidic rainwater seeped through the ground, slowly dissolving the soluble limestone bedrock to carve massive caverns.
Mangrove forests in Olango Island protect coastlines because their dense, tangled root systems slow down wave energy, causing suspended sand and mud to settle.
The Banaue Rice Terraces prevent mountain erosion because stone-walled paddies slow down heavy rain runoff, allowing water to safely seep into the soil.
Coastal areas experience sea breezes during the day because land heats up faster than the ocean, causing cooler, heavier sea air to rush inland.
Coral atolls form around volcanic islands because the coral grows upward as the central volcano slowly sinks and erodes beneath the ocean surface.
